newsitem.title: FRANCE: Albright warm in style, not substance with France.
newsitem.headline: Albright warm in style, not substance with France.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, kissed by French leaders and chatting in French, warmed the tone if not the substance of Washington's often stormy relations with France on Monday.

"What do you want me to tell you? It was good," Albright told reporters in French after a 90-minute meeting with President Jacques Chirac which officials said covered NATO enlargement and reform, the Middle East, China and Africa.
Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said there was "a very good attitude. We must make this spirit of friendship prevail, even if there are sometimes differences of approach."
She quoted Albright as saying she wanted to turn over a new page in the relationship, strained by disputes last year over NATO, Africa, the United Nations and the Middle East.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, determined to make a good start with his new counterpart after a bittersweet farewell to her predecessor, Warren Christopher, kissed Albright four times when she arrived at the Elysee presidential palace.
For good measure, Chirac kissed her hand on the way out.
But there was no sign that they had narrowed U.S.-French differences over the sharing out of NATO commands or the path to a new relationship between the West and Russia.

Colonna said France was still weighing the idea of a "big five" summit to help overcome Russian hostility to the eastward expansion of NATO, despite angering smaller allies like Italy, but Washington "preferred to concentrate on other channels".

She said they did not directly address France's call for the United States to hand over NATO's southern command, which controls the Mediterranean, to a European. Albright reaffirmed Washington's refusal in a weekend French newspaper interview.

Colonna quoted Chirac as saying Paris was ready to consider returning to the alliance's integrated command, which it quit in 1966 in protest at U.S. domination, if the current reforms allowed the creation of a real European defence pillar in NATO.

On a first, nine-nation, foreign trip since taking office, Albright was keen to make a new start after a stormy patch in relations with the French, who resent what Paris officials call America's "velvet hegemony" in world affairs.

In linguistic goodwill gestures, the new secretary spoke in French at a memorial ceremony for the late U.S. ambassador Pamela Harriman, who died in Paris this month. She also conducted part of the meeting with Chirac in French.
On the key aim of Albright's 11-day tour -- the enlargement of NATO to admit former communist central and east European countries -- France and Washington are in broad agreement.

They agree that NATO's summit in Madrid in July should invite the first former Warsaw Pact countries to negotiate membership of the Western defence alliance. But France wants Romania added to Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and possibly Slovenia as candidates for admission in the first wave.
In Bonn earlier, Albright stressed broad agreement with Germany on plans to persuade Moscow to accept NATO enlargement.
But German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said Bonn remained interested in the French idea of a five-nation mini-summit on NATO expansion to smoothe Russian acceptance.

France agrees with Washington that Russia cannot have a veto over NATO membership or future European security arrangements, but it is more sympathetic to Moscow's demand for binding commitments in a charter on future ties to the West.
Diplomats say the differences reflect deeper French concern that Washington should not monopolise the negotiation of the future NATO-Russian relationship.

Albright, who is to visit NATO headquarters in Brussels on Tuesday, also discussed the war in crumbling Zaire and the Great Lakes region of central Africa and the need for dialogue with China on human rights.
Colonna said Chirac warned of possible "grave consequences" if borders were called into question in central Africa.

Paris and Washington have backed different sides in the conflict but have moved closer together in the last two weeks in opposing foreign intervention in Zaire and coordinating their separate plans for an inter-African peace-keeping force.
